name: Icall wireless perm machine

lead: The Icall wireless perm machine was a 1930s salon device that gave women a permanent wave using heated curlers. Its main change was the "wireless" design, in which a cord supported the weight of the heater so no electrical connection sat near the head.

It helped people look better by giving hair lasting curl and volume for weeks or months, in the style of its era. The history is documented in accounts of permanent waving rather than in clinical research.

paras: In salon use, hair was wound on rollers, chemically treated and heated by the machine's heaters for a set time; a timer on the 1934 model adjusted processing for hair type. Modern perms use chemical solutions and do not need such machines.
Early permanent-wave machines caused scalp burns and hair damage, and electrical accidents worried clients, which motivated wireless designs.

chain: Hair wound on rollers and heated by the machine
angle.text: The machine set curl into hair that lasted for weeks or months, giving the waved styles fashionable in the 1930s. It is of historical interest today.

lead: The Icall wireless perm machine was a permanent-wave device made by the Icall brand in the 1930s. Isidoro Calvete, a Spanish immigrant, designed a practical heater in 1917 and also made machines under the Icall name, competing with the Eugene machines sold by Eugene Suter, who had patented the design [1].

An Icall machine from 1934 used Bakelite heaters and a timer that adjusted for hair type. The company's "wireless" system replaced the electric lead with a cord supporting the heater's weight so that no electrical potential was near the head, a response to accidents that had made clients wary of electrical perms [1].

Perms gave hair durable waves, which was how people of the era styled for volume and shape. Methods that followed included steam-based systems, machineless chemical pads, the heatless overnight wave of 1931 and the cold wave of 1938 that became the precursor of modern perms [1]. No clinical studies of the machine exist.

paras: Karl Nessler demonstrated an electric permanent wave in 1905 using heated brass rollers and sodium hydroxide, and a single perm took about six hours [1]. In 1917 Calvete designed a heater with two windings inside an aluminium tube; Suter patented it and sold it as the Eugene brand, while Calvete produced competing machines under the Icall name [1].
Later Icall designs added croquignole heaters and a chandelier-style support [1].

Nessler's first trials on his wife burned her hair off and caused scalp burns, and electrical accidents with the equipment of the era worried clients. Steam-based alternatives carried a scalding risk [1].

timeline.event: Karl Nessler demonstrates an electric permanent-wave machine [1].
Calvete designs a practical perm heater; Suter patents it [1].
Icall machine with Bakelite heaters and a timer is introduced [1].
Arnold Willatt's cold wave uses no heat or machines [1].
